qt: to the Vice-President of the Commission / High Representative of the Union for Foreign Affairs and Security Policy Michał Dworczyk (ECR) Subject:

The report on human resources in the European External Action Service (EEAS) for 20231 once again reveals a persistent lack of adequate representation of staff from Member States that, like Poland, joined the EU in 2004. This imbalance is particularly apparent in the top posts of the EEAS. Parliament has repeatedly called for full geographical balance in EU diplomacy. In addition, the rules governing the functioning of and the recruitment of staff to the EEAS impose an obligation on the EEAS to strive to achieve this balance23. Especially now, with a war being waged in Ukraine, the voices of representatives of countries bordering the front line, such as Poland, are invaluable in view of their geographical proximity to and historical experience with Russia. Such insights are essential for effective European policy-making in the current climate and are also important for the functioning of the EEAS and EU diplomacy. 1.

What specific steps does the Vice-President/High Representative of the EU plan to take in order to effectively address these imbalances which, despite 20 years of EU enlargement, remain unresolved, in particular at management levels and among heads of EU delegations and offices?
Does the Vice-President/High Representative feel that the national composition of selection boards may influence the recruitment process by favouring certain nationalities?
Is this process subject to any scrutiny? If not, does the Vice-President/High Representative plan to take action to ensure adequate nationality representation on EEAS selection boards?
at: (English version) to the Vice-President of the Commission/High Representative of the Union for Foreign Affairs and Security Policy Michał Dworczyk (ECR) (19 December 2024) Subject: The need to work towards achieving a geographical and nationality balance among staff in the European External Action Service The report on human resources in the European External Action Service (EEAS) for 2023 (1) once again reveals a persistent lack of adequate representation of staff from Member States that, like Poland, joined the EU in 2004. This imbalance is particularly apparent in the top posts of the EEAS. Parliament has repeatedly called for full geographical balance in EU diplomacy. In addition, the rules governing the functioning of and the recruitment of staff to the EEAS impose an obligation on the EEAS to strive to achieve this balance (2) (3). Especially now, with a war being waged in Ukraine, the voices of representatives of countries bordering the front line, such as Poland, are invaluable in view of their geographical proximity to and historical experience with Russia. Such insights are essential for effective European policy-making in the current climate and are also important for the functioning of the EEAS and EU diplomacy. 1. What specific steps does the Vice-President/High Representative of the EU plan to take in order to effectively address these imbalances which, despite 20 years of EU enlargement, remain unresolved, in particular at management levels and among heads of EU delegations and offices? 2. Does the Vice-President/High Representative feel that the national composition of selection boards may influence the recruitment process by favouring certain nationalities? 3. Is this process subject to any scrutiny? If not, does the Vice-President/High Representative plan to take action to ensure adequate nationality representation on EEAS selection boards? (12 March 2025) 1. European External Action Service (EEAS) recruitments and selections are based on merit whilst ensuring adequate geographical and gender balance (1). While ‘no posts shall be reserved for nationals of any specific Member State’ (2), current efforts continue to focus on achieving a more balanced representation from Member States, including of those who joined after 2004 (EU-13). Measures include outreach initiatives aimed at attracting qualified candidates, collaboration with national authorities aimed at increasing the quantity and quality of applications as well as a constant monitoring of the geographical balance both at management and non-management level. The share of staff holding EU-13 nationalities reached 23% in the EEAS in 2023, slightly exceeding the EU-13’s 22.6% share in the total EU population. 2. As of 1 September 2024 (3), all Member States but one (Hungary) are represented at the level of EU Ambassador or Deputy Head of Delegation. This is the result of proactive EEAS action, including through steady exchanges with Member States, dedicated outreach events and information sessions aimed at under-represented Member States. 3. The composition of the selection boards for management posts in headquarters and delegations is detailed in the EEAS Decision on the Consultative Committee on Appointments (4), which provides, inter alia, that its members are representatives of the EEAS, the Commission, the Council and two Member States.
